topic: Law, Rights and Safeguarding in Learning Disability
title: Equality Act 2010 and the duty to adjust
blurb: Use the Equality Act 2010 to identify the reasonable adjustments a person with a learning disability is owed and the kinds of discrimination to challenge.
question: Kofi, 34, has a learning disability and cannot read. A clinic policy discharges anyone who misses two appointments, and Kofi has missed two because the letters were in standard print. What does the Equality Act 2010 require of the clinic?

teach.h: Disability in law, and why it matters here
teach.body: Under the Equality Act 2010, a person has a disability if they have a physical or mental impairment that has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. Long-term means it has lasted, or is likely to last, at least 12 months. A learning disability will usually meet this definition. In plain English: the Act protects people with a learning disability from unfair treatment and requires services to change how they work.

teach.h: The three requirements of the duty (s20)
head: Requirement
Means
LD example
rows: Change a policy or way of working
Quiet room instead of busy waiting area
Provide extra help or a service
Easy read letter, longer appointment support
teach.caption: Where the first or third requirement concerns information, reasonable steps include providing it in an accessible format (s20(6)).

items.label: requirements: practice, physical feature, auxiliary aid
the disabled person cannot be charged for an adjustment (s20(7))
for services the duty is anticipatory: plan before people arrive
failing to make a reasonable adjustment is discrimination

teach.body: For service providers and public functions, including the NHS, the duty is owed to disabled people generally (Schedule 2). That means services must think ahead about the barriers people with a learning disability are likely to face and plan adjustments before anyone asks, such as easy read information, flexible booking and quiet spaces. Waiting for a request or a complaint does not meet the duty.

teach.h: Scenario: Kofi and the missed appointments
teach.body: Kofi, 34, cannot read and missed two appointments sent by standard letter. The clinic's discharge rule is a provision, criterion or practice that puts him at a substantial disadvantage. The nurse re-books him, flags that letters should be in easy read with pictures, adds phone or text reminders his supporter can help with, and records the adjustment so it follows him. Kofi is not charged for any of it.

rows.label: Direct (s13)
values: Less favourable treatment because of disability

rows.label: Arising from (s15)
values: Unfavourable treatment for something caused by the disability
Barring a man for distressed shouting

rows.label: Indirect (s19)
values: A rule for all that disadvantages disabled people

teach.caption: s15 can be justified if the treatment is a proportionate means of a legitimate aim.

items: Public bodies, including NHS trusts, must have due regard to eliminating discrimination.
They must have due regard to advancing equality of opportunity, including meeting disabled people's needs.
They must have due regard to fostering good relations between groups.
In practice: considering people with a learning disability when designing or changing services.

teach.text: Do not confuse the duty to adjust with a favour. A reasonable adjustment is a legal duty, it cannot be charged for, and for services it must be planned in advance. Also, 'treating everyone the same' can itself be discrimination when the same rule disadvantages a person with a learning disability.

items: Disability: impairment with a substantial, long-term (12 months) adverse effect on day-to-day activities.
s20: change practices, alter physical features, provide auxiliary aids (including accessible formats).
No charge to the disabled person (s20(7)); failure to adjust is discrimination (s21).
For services the duty is anticipatory: plan before people attend.
Know s13 direct, s15 arising from disability, s19 indirect and the s149 public sector equality duty.

summary: You can now name the three reasonable adjustment requirements, apply them to a person with a learning disability, and explain that the duty is anticipatory and free to the person. You can also tell direct discrimination from discrimination arising from disability and indirect discrimination.

A.q: A learning disability liaison nurse is teaching ward staff about section 20 of the Equality Act 2010. Which set describes the three requirements of the duty to make reasonable adjustments?
options: Assess capacity, act in best interests, choose the least restrictive option
Change practices, alter physical features, provide auxiliary aids
Identify, record and flag needs, then share and meet them
Prevent harm, protect the person, act proportionately
A.why: s20(3)-(5): change a provision, criterion or practice; remove or alter a physical feature; provide an auxiliary aid.

whyNot.0: These are Mental Capacity Act principles, not the s20 requirements.
whyNot.2: These are steps of the Accessible Information Standard.
whyNot.3: These echo the safeguarding principles, not the s20 duty.

A.q: Ruth, 41, has a learning disability and needs a double-length appointment and an easy read explanation of her procedure. The clinic manager asks whether Ruth can be asked to pay towards the extra time. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes, a contribution can be asked for the extra time
Yes, if the cost is disproportionate for the clinic
No, but her support provider can be asked to pay
No, she must not be charged for the adjustment
A.why: s20(7): a disabled person must not be required to pay any of the costs of complying with the duty to make reasonable adjustments.

whyNot.0: The Act forbids passing adjustment costs to the disabled person.
whyNot.1: Cost can affect what is reasonable, but a reasonable adjustment is still not charged to the person.
whyNot.2: Shifting the cost to her support provider is not the clinic meeting its own duty.

A.q: A GP practice sends Dev, who has a learning disability, his screening invitation in easy read with pictures. Which reasonable adjustment requirement does this meet?
options: Changing the screening eligibility criteria
Removing or altering a physical feature
Providing an auxiliary aid
The public sector equality duty
A.why: Easy read information is an auxiliary aid (s20(5)); s20(6) adds that where a requirement concerns information, reasonable steps include providing it in an accessible format.

whyNot.0: Nothing about who is eligible for screening changed; what changed was the format of the information Dev received.
whyNot.1: Physical features are building or environment features.
whyNot.3: The PSED (s149) is a separate duty on public bodies, not one of the three s20 requirements.

B.q: An outpatient manager says, 'We make reasonable adjustments for people with a learning disability as soon as they ask.' Which response best reflects the Equality Act 2010?
options: The duty is anticipatory: plan adjustments in advance
The duty starts when a carer requests it in writing
The duty applies once a disability is formally diagnosed
The duty is met if staff respond within 48 hours
B.why: For service providers the duty is owed to disabled people generally (Sch 2), so it is anticipatory: services must plan adjustments before people attend.

whyNot.1: The duty does not wait for a written request from anyone.
whyNot.2: The duty is owed to disabled people generally; it is not triggered by a formal diagnosis.
whyNot.3: There is no 48-hour response standard; adjustments should already be planned.

B.q: Carl, 29, is autistic and has a learning disability. A council gym bars him after he became distressed and shouted when the music was too loud. Which form of discrimination is most likely?
options: Direct discrimination because of disability
Discrimination arising from disability
Harassment related to disability
Victimisation for making a complaint
B.why: s15: he was treated unfavourably because of something (distressed shouting) arising in consequence of his disability; this is unlawful unless it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.

whyNot.0: Direct discrimination is less favourable treatment because of disability itself, not because of something arising from it.
whyNot.2: Harassment is unwanted conduct that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment.
whyNot.3: Victimisation needs a protected act, such as a complaint under the Act.

B.q: Kofi, 34, has a learning disability and cannot read. Under clinic policy he is due to be discharged after missing two appointments sent by standard letter. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Discharge him and ask his GP to refer him again
Keep the policy and send the next letter by recorded post
Adjust the policy for Kofi and use phone or text reminders
Ask his family to sign a promise that he will attend
B.why: The discharge rule is a provision, criterion or practice that puts Kofi at a substantial disadvantage. Adjusting it and using accessible reminders meets s20(3) and (5).

whyNot.0: Discharging him applies the very rule that disadvantages him.
whyNot.1: Recorded post is still standard print that he cannot read.
whyNot.3: This places the burden on his family instead of the service adjusting.

C.q: A trust board is redesigning outpatient booking so that appointments can be made online. A learning disability nurse sits on the project group. Which legal duty requires the board to consider the effect on people with a learning disability now?
options: The safeguarding duty under section 42 of the Care Act
The duty of candour under regulation 20
The public sector equality duty under section 149
The best interests duty under section 4 of the MCA
C.why: s149 requires public bodies to have due regard to eliminating discrimination and advancing equality of opportunity when exercising their functions, including redesigning services.

whyNot.0: Section 42 concerns enquiries into abuse or neglect of individual adults.
whyNot.1: The duty of candour concerns openness after notifiable safety incidents.
whyNot.3: Best interests decisions concern an individual who lacks capacity.

C.q: Tina, 26, has a learning disability and becomes very distressed in noisy waiting rooms; she has left twice without being seen. She needs an outpatient scan. What is the best adjustment to plan?
options: Ask her to arrive early so she can settle in the waiting room
Book the first slot of the day with a quiet place to wait
Prescribe a sedative to take before every hospital visit
Advise her to bring two carers to keep her in the room
C.why: A first appointment and a quiet waiting space remove the barrier (noise and waiting), combining a change in practice with avoiding a physical feature.

whyNot.0: Arriving early increases her time in the environment that distresses her.
whyNot.2: Sedation does not remove the barrier and is not the least restrictive adjustment.
whyNot.3: This tries to contain Tina instead of adjusting the service.

C.q: A surgeon tells Amir, 45, who has a learning disability, that he will not be offered a knee replacement 'because people like him cannot manage rehabilitation', without assessing him. Which form of discrimination does this most closely describe?
options: Direct discrimination because of his disability
Indirect discrimination from a general policy
A failure to provide an auxiliary aid
Discrimination arising from a past complaint
C.why: s13: treating Amir less favourably because of his disability itself, based on an assumption about 'people like him', is direct discrimination.

whyNot.1: Indirect discrimination arises from a rule applied to everyone; here he is singled out because of his disability.
whyNot.2: Auxiliary aids may help rehabilitation, but the core wrong is refusing treatment because of disability.
whyNot.3: Treatment because of a complaint would be victimisation, and there was no complaint.

reteach.title: Find the barrier, then name the fix
reteach.question: How do you turn the s20 duty into a practical plan for one person?

blocks.body: Ask what stops this person getting the same service as anyone else. A rule (missed-appointment policy) needs changing. A place (a noisy waiting room) needs avoiding or altering. A missing support (easy read, a longer slot) needs providing. Then plan it ahead, record it and do not charge for it.

blocks.text: A request is not the starting point for services: the duty is anticipatory, owed to disabled people generally.

explain.body: A physical or mental impairment with a substantial and long-term adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities (s6). Long-term means it has lasted at least 12 months, is likely to last that long or for the rest of the person's life, or is likely to recur.

test.q: Under the Equality Act 2010, what does 'long-term' mean in the definition of disability?
options: It has lasted or is likely to last at least 12 months
It has lasted at least 6 months with a diagnosis
It began before the person reached the age of 18
It affects at least two areas of day-to-day activity
test.why: Sch 1 para 2: long-term means it has lasted at least 12 months, or is likely to last at least 12 months or for the rest of the person's life; an effect likely to recur also counts.

whyNot.1: Six months is not the statutory period, and diagnosis is not required.
whyNot.2: Onset before adulthood is part of the policy definition of learning disability, not the Act's long-term test.
whyNot.3: That mixes up the 'day-to-day activities' part of the definition with long-term; the Act sets no count of areas, and long-term is about how long the effect lasts.

explain.body: Change a provision, criterion or practice; remove, alter or avoid a physical feature; provide an auxiliary aid, including information in an accessible format. No charge to the person.

test.q: A hospital moves Jay's appointment from a crowded, echoing waiting area to a quiet side room because noise distresses him. Which requirement is this?
options: Providing an auxiliary aid
Avoiding a physical feature
Advancing equality of opportunity
Changing a criterion for treatment
test.why: The crowded, echoing area is a physical feature; s20(4) includes avoiding it.

whyNot.0: An auxiliary aid is extra help or equipment, such as easy read or a communication aid.
whyNot.2: This is part of the public sector equality duty, not an s20 requirement.
whyNot.3: No treatment criterion was changed; the environment was.

explain.body: For services, the duty is owed to disabled people generally, so adjustments are planned in advance. Costs cannot be passed to the disabled person (s20(7)).

test.q: A dental practice wants to start offering easy read leaflets and longer appointments for people with a learning disability. When should it put these in place?
options: After the first complaint from a patient
When a patient brings a written request
Once a patient's carer explains the need
In advance, before patients need them
test.why: The duty for service providers is anticipatory (Sch 2), so adjustments should be planned before they are needed.

whyNot.0: Waiting for a complaint fails the anticipatory duty.
whyNot.1: A written request is not required for the duty to apply.
whyNot.2: Individual needs still matter, but the service should already have adjustments ready.

explain.body: s15: treating a person unfavourably because of something arising from their disability (such as distressed behaviour or missed letters), unless it is a proportionate means of a legitimate aim, or the provider did not know and could not reasonably have known.

test.q: A café bars Leo, who has a learning disability, because he talks loudly when excited, a feature of his disability. Which section of the Equality Act is most relevant?
options: Section 13
Section 19
Section 15
Section 149
test.why: s15 covers unfavourable treatment because of something arising in consequence of a disability.

whyNot.0: s13 is direct discrimination because of the disability itself.
whyNot.1: s19 is indirect discrimination from a rule applied to everyone.
whyNot.3: s149 is the public sector equality duty, which does not apply to a private café's treatment of one person.
